Los Cóbanos is a small fishing community on the coast of the western department of Sonsonate, located 11 kilometers east of the municipality and port of Acajutla.
In its surroundings there are several paradisiacal beaches, which, because of their honey-colored sand, coral composition, calm water, and the rock formations that rise along the entire coast, constitute a truly unique place in El Salvador.
The general area of Los Cóbanos is a zone of 264 square kilometers of marine ecosystem under environmental protection, due to its richness and natural diversity.
Surfing has not been very popular in this place, because the surrounding reef forms a kind of breakwater that creates a wide confined water area. However, there are spots such as the nearby Salinitas beach, where channels form between the reefs, creating small but consistent waves, ideal for SUP surfing or paddle-boarding.
Less known are some rock formations, about 800 meters from the shore, which on days of large swells produce waves of the type known as “outer reef,” and can reach up to 10 feet in height (3.5 meters), disappearing when they encounter deeper water after running about 200 meters. These spots can only be accessed by boat and under the guidance of a local guide.
Between November and February the area is ideal for tank diving, as there are dozens of volcanic reefs and some shipwrecks, whose marine life and formations are stunning. There are also coastal zones suitable for snorkeling and kayaking.
This area is famous for blue-water fishing, because a few kilometers offshore there are deep marine trenches where coveted species such as golden fish, sailfish, wahoo, tuna and marlin take refuge and feed. Local boat operators offer their vessels, equipment and expertise to organize a day of fishing that can be unforgettable.
A special attraction is that whale sightings are common in Los Cóbanos, especially of the humpback species. Scientific studies have established that this is a nutrient-rich zone that attracts these huge mammals, which feed and rest in its waters during the months of January and February, before continuing the migration that takes them from Alaska to Ecuador. Locals offer tours to enjoy this unique spectacle.
This tourist destination has experienced huge growth and development, so there is an increasing offering of accommodations, food and other services.
To reach Los Cóbanos from San Salvador, take the Pan-American Highway toward Sonsonate, then turn toward Acajutla, passing the Kilo 5 turnoff; 3 kilometers later you will find the turnoff to Los Cóbanos, which is 7 kilometers away.

From the Port of La Libertad westward, traveling the Litoral highway, with its impressive cliffs and views, is a true spectacle. But immediately after passing the first of its five tunnels, carved in the heart of these emerald-colored mountains, it will be impossible not to fix your gaze on the perfect swell that breaks hundreds of meters below, on the beach known as K59.

After this initial impression, just under a kilometer further along the highway you will find the trail that leads to this wave paradise, distinguished by a massive split cliff on the left and a sea of gray river stones on the right; a setting that makes its beautiful volcanic black-sand beach stand out.

Like most surf spots in El Salvador, K59 is a rocky point that receives the swells of the southern Pacific Ocean directly, creating a fast-wave machine with a right-hand break, long rides, tubular sections, and a wide, steep wall.

Between March and August this beach can produce waves up to 12 feet high (4 meters). The rest of the year, especially between November and December, the wave size decreases, though because of its rocky bottom and wave shape it is not suitable for beginners.

K59 beach is surrounded by mountains and coastal forests that are part of the southern mountain range of El Salvador, long known as the balsam coast because of the plantations of these trees, which have been harvested since colonial times to extract their valuable amber liquid.

This area has just begun its tourism development, so there is little tourist and surfer traffic; however, there are already some camp-style accommodations for surfers, as well as numerous houses for rent. Nevertheless, it only takes 20 minutes by car or bus to reach the Port of La Libertad, where travelers can stock up on everything they need.

To get to K59 from San Salvador, take the highway to the Port of La Libertad, and when you arrive, turn right onto the Litoral highway, continuing past the first tunnel.

El Cocal has become a popular destination for surfing. Conveniently located just 2 kilometers west of the Port of La Libertad.
As with most surf beaches in El Salvador, El Cocal is a medium-sized rocky point break, in this case carved by the mouth of a small river, which generates right-hand waves whose size and power depend on the swell conditions that hit the Salvadoran coast from the south.
Between March and September, this spot can produce swells up to 10 feet high (3.5 meters), long rides, wide and steep walls, and tubular sections that die out on the long volcanic sand beach that lies to the east. At those times it becomes a powerful and demanding wave, suitable for expert surfers. In periods of small waves it tends to become reluctant to break, so it is important to know its temperament.
In any case surfing is recommended at high tide, due to the rocky and shallow bottom.
In the heart of Surf City, this area has developed rapidly. Hotels and accommodations are multiplying, and just a few steps away there are dozens of restaurants and other services, including the offerings of the Port of La Libertad.
Although the surf zone at El Cocal is not suitable for swimmers, because of its rocky topography, on its sides and just a few meters away there are two beautiful beaches: San Blas to the west and the also-called El Cocal beach, which connects with Conchalío beach to the east. Both have volcanic sand and numerous additional attractions.
To get to El Cocal from San Salvador, take the highway to the Port of La Libertad, then the impressive bypass Camino a Surf City; from this road you can see the beaches of La Libertad, and then continue less than half a kilometer on the Litoral road westward.

There are several legends that tell its story; one of them says that during colonial times the property belonged to the Renderos family, from which the name Los Planes de Renderos comes.
The daughter of this family, María de La Paz, was courted by the devil himself, which is why they decided to hunt him down. One night, after having courted the young woman, the demon was pursued and, when he saw himself trapped, he broke the cliff to escape through the middle. Since then it has been known as “La Puerta del Diablo,” because of the curious arch shape formed by the two high rocks that make it up.

Other accounts mention that this place formed at the end of the 18th century, a period in which three meteorological catastrophes occurred on the coast in the years 1772, 1774 and 1781, causing severe storms and floods that created that stone formation. Later, another heavy storm in 1906 caused large landslides, permanently separating the two enormous cliffs. This rocky area has three outcrops known by locals as: “El Chulo,” “El Chulito,” and “El Chulón.”

Acajutla is an active municipality and the main industrial seaport of El Salvador. It is located in the western department of Sonsonate.
The beach of Acajutla is situated next to the bustling urban area of this port city, but when it comes to surfing, other nearby beaches and spots should be mentioned.
A notable fact is that this part of the Salvadoran coast faces east, not south like most beaches in the country; this means the area is not as exposed to swells that hit from the southern Pacific Ocean. Therefore, the waves in Acajutla are not as powerful or large, although one should not be complacent, as each locality has its own character. It can even be said that there are still waves to discover in this region.
Next to the industrial pier, heading east, is Las Flores beach, a gentle and friendly right-breaking wave that has become a true magnet for SUP surfers and longboarders. It is important to note that it only works at high tide, as its rocky bottom becomes dangerously exposed at low and medium tides.
Immediately after Las Flores, still to the east, is Punta Negra or Negrei, as locals call it. It is unique for being the only left-breaking point in El Salvador. Its wave can become powerful and rewarding. It works on all tides, but at the lowest tide it tends to close.
To the west of the Acajutla industrial pier there are also beaches where surfing is possible, although they are more suitable for body surfing.
La Bocana is a “beach break” located on the western side of the Acajutla artisanal pier. It breaks both left and right, and its characteristics are speed, short length, tube shape, and abrupt closures.
On days of strong swells, the artisanal pier produces a long, slow, gentle left wave, ideal for riding on a longboard or a SUP; however, one should avoid connecting with the “beach break” to prevent a dangerous closure.
After La Bocana comes La Pilsener beach, another “beach break,” less tubular but always fast and steep. It only breaks at medium tides.
Because it is a port city, the general area of Acajutla has a good level of development and, consequently, many services for visitors. There are numerous hotels, some beachfront, rental houses, as well as restaurants, bars, and other attractions. Connectivity is also good.
To reach Acajutla from San Salvador, take the Pan-American Highway and then the road to Sonsonate. Before entering that city, take the road to Acajutla and continue until the signage indicates you have arrived.

Costa del Sol beach is a natural gem located in the department of La Paz, in the central region of El Salvador.
Unlike the rocky formations and cliffs that characterize the beaches of the east and west of the country, this area is surrounded by a beautiful valley, where it is easy to spot some of the most beautiful and majestic Salvadoran volcanoes, at whose feet lie swaths of winding canals and other local crops.
Costa del Sol offers visitors a perfect combination of attractions that make it a world-class beach destination. If you are looking for a place to enjoy the sun from sunrise to sunset, an endless white-sand beach, all types of accommodations, a wide showcase of Salvadoran and international cuisine, and the added appeal of being surrounded by an immense navigable estuary and waves for great surfing, this should be your choice.
The beach is 15 kilometers long, and regarding surfing it is characterized by sandbanks that form across the entire breaking zone; they generate fast waves that break both to the right and to the left, usually tubular, and truly challenging when a light north wind blows, raising their crests and increasing the wall size for maneuvers, which can reach up to 9 feet (3 meters) in height.
The best time of year to surf Costa del Sol is from November to January, when the southern Pacific swells are not so large and powerful, allowing the wave to break with less speed and more smoothness. Small, foamy ripples also form, ideal for beginners to start practicing this exciting sport.
As a complement to the great surf, Costa del Sol has an enviable hotel and private-house rental offering. There are numerous restaurants along the boulevard that crosses it, some very typical under a palm-leaf canopy, and others truly gourmet.
The beach is bordered by the immense Jaltepeque estuary, populated by intricate and pristine mangroves, ideal for SUP, kayaking, sailing, fishing, and ski; or for renting a small boat and taking a pleasant ride. San Andrés is one of the largest pre-hispanic centers in El Salvador. It would have been a regional capital between 600 and 900 A.D. This ancient community covered a total of 200 hectares or more, and consisted of a monumental center surrounded by a broad common residential area.
The site includes an acropolis, which is an elevated plaza with pyramids and residential houses on the upper level. There is also a large plaza on the north side where other pyramids stand, including one shaped like a bell. Most of the structures are open to the public, making your tour more entertaining and filled with beautiful green scenery.
According to researchers, in the surrounding area, small huts housed the farmers who harvested the main crops, such as corn, beans and pipián. All the buildings were constructed of adobe blocks, except two structures that were built with volcanic tuff blocks, locally known as talpetate. The details of the acropolis layout and everything found are displayed in the site museum.
It is believed that San Andrés came to dominate the Zapotitán valley, and some neighboring areas, such as the Las Hamacas valley, now San Salvador.
San Andrés is usually hot, so it is best to wear appropriate clothing and shoes. Do not forget to bring a hat. It is also recommended that you bring your own food, as the site has picnic areas and a small café where you can find water, sodas, hydrating drinks, and snacks.

El Zonte is one of the most iconic surf destinations in El Salvador.
This small coastal community is located at kilometer 53 of the Litoral highway, in the municipality of Chiltiupán, La Libertad.
The place retains its original bohemian and beachy style, even though its tourist services have expanded.
The area adjacent to the El Zonte river offers numerous hostels, rental houses, hotels and restaurants, as well as surfboard rentals and surf lessons.
Beyond the small estuary, to the west, there are private ranches and several small hotels, where you can also spend the day.
On the eastern end, several higher-quality and more modern hotels and restaurants are concentrated, including a surf training center, the only one of its kind in the world.
El Zonte has several sections for surfing. The most popular is the punta, a rocky formation that breaks to the right, generating a fast, long-line wave, occasionally tubular; it can reach up to 10 feet in height (3.5 meters) and projects onto a small beach that has a sea stack at its eastern end, which should be avoided on days of large swells.
From the punta toward the west there are two other sections: the first is a left-hand wave that forms over the rocky bottom at the river mouth; it is a fast, long, powerful wave.
Then follows a beach break area, whose typical characteristics are speed and steepness, a short line, and tubular sections that crash onto the sandy beach.
El Zonte offers a striking landscape; sea stacks and rock tongues that plunge into the sea frame its boundaries. There are two volcanic black-sand beaches, separated by the river and its small estuary. Meanwhile, interesting caves in the western sector of the beach provide the perfect backdrop for a photograph.
Getting to El Zonte is easy: from San Salvador take the road to Puerto de La Libertad, then join the bypass Camino a Surf City, and upon reaching the Litoral highway, continue westward to kilometer 53, where the signage will indicate that you have arrived.

The wave at Punta Roca, or “La Punta,” as local surfers call it, breaks to the right over a rocky bottom and is considered by experts to be one of the 10 best surf spots in the world. Because of its power and speed, this wave is suitable for advanced and expert surfers.

But if you want to experience its epic character, you should visit between March and August, when swells generated by storms in the southern Pacific Ocean reach El Salvador. Capable of handling swells up to 12 feet high (4 m), its best conditions are when the swell is between 4 and 8 feet (1.5 to 2.5 m) and the direction is from the southwest.
Punta Roca works at any tide, but you must be careful of its rocky bottom, especially the formation locals call “mamá roca,” a rock outcrop that protrudes from the water at low tide.

El K61 is the beach that follows K59, heading westward in El Salvador.

On the immense rocky seabed that projects out to sea, two wave sections form. But when this same section approaches the shoreline, the wave becomes gentler and slower, ideal for riding longboards, doing SUP surf, or for beginners.
If the swell is too large at other points, K61 usually shows a milder, even epic side, with heights of 2 to 8 feet (0.5 to 2.5 meters). You must take into account that the beach is covered with thousands of river stones, and there are sea-urchin colonies in the water, so extra caution is needed when entering.

Come see the artificial lake of El Salvador!
Just as it reads, Lago Suchitlán is a man-made work created to harness hydraulic energy and provide a source of drinking water. Its creation dates back to 1973-1976 with the construction of the Central Hidroeléctrica Cerrón Grande.
Although it is an artificial river, its contribution is enormous, as its channel produces the largest amount of electric power for El Salvador. However, it also has key tourist aspects for the area. Many come to the lake to fish, ride a boat, or cross it by kayak.
Its name was created by Alejandro Cotto, one of the greatest cultural references of the place, which arose by mixing the initials of Suchitoto and the last letters of Cuscatlán. This artificial beauty is so large that it is located among three departments: Chalatenango, Cuscatlán and Cabañas.
If you want to learn more about the beauties surrounding this lake, board a boat and visit the most beautiful and hidden islands the area has. Among them you can find: Isla Los Pájaros, Isla Los Enamorados, Isla El Chaparral, Isla El Ermitaño, among others. You cannot miss these unique landscapes.

Taquillo complex is a protected natural area located in the municipality of La Libertad Costa, in the department of La Libertad.
The zone has the largest extent of deciduous forests, meaning they lose their leaves at some point of the year, which turn to vegetation when they reach the cliffs that overlook the sea.
It is a region with great natural diversity, and one of its rarities is the existence of the Aztec snail, locally known as “jute dye”, because of the milky substance it secretes and can be used as a natural dye. Also noteworthy is the presence of the purple snail, an endangered species.
The most well-known beach in the area is Shalpa, a small natural and virgin paradise, which stands out for its isolation, rocky reefs, and lush vegetation.
Shalpa is an extraordinary beach. There are elevated rock formations that offer beautiful views, while its dark-sand coast contrasts with the rocks that jut out from the shoreline and the sea. In some spots, salt-water pools form, which can be enjoyed at low tide.
The swell is usually calm at this beach. It is not so suitable for surfing, but the right tide and wave direction can create conditions to hop on a board or a SUP and enjoy a nice session in calm waters amid a breathtaking landscape.
If you obtain the corresponding permits from the Ministry of the Environment, you can organize an unforgettable camping trip at the site.
Taquillo is an exceptional place for ecotourism and feeling like you are in a lost world. Because of these same characteristics there are few services in the area, but its proximity to other more developed beaches and to the port of La Libertad, which is only 25 kilometers away, makes it easy to get supplies or return to “civilization”.
Due to its beauty and tranquility, the offering of accommodations in the area has been increasing.
To get there from San Salvador, take the road to the port of La Libertad, then the bypass Camino a Surf City, and continue on the Litoral road heading west; after tunnel one, look for the sign indicating you have arrived at Taquillo, then you can choose to go up to the town on your right, or down to the coast. Explore several Maya structures, including a ballcourt and temples, at the Tazumal Archaeological Park in Chalchuapa.
Tazumal was the site of an important and sophisticated Maya settlement that existed around the years 100 to 1200 A.D. After a long occupation, the site was abandoned around 1200 A.D. and is now a treasure full of history.
Structure 1 is one of the main ones, standing 24 meters tall with 13 construction phases dated between 100 and 800 A.D. The main building is a large rectangular Maya-style structure topped by a temple. It has 13 concentric layers, and the upper levels form, in addition to the pyramid, a ballcourt and a water-drainage system.
One of the most important sculptures found at this site is the Tazumal Stele, measuring 2.65 meters high and 1.16 meters wide.
Among the activities you can do is a guided visit to the Illustrative Museum, which contains an extensive infographic with detailed information about the park’s history and discovery.

San Blas is one of the most beautiful beaches in El Salvador, and it has the greatest potential as a tourist destination and for surfing.
Located only 3 kilometers west of the Port of La Libertad, and practically at the exit of the modern bypass Camino a Surf City, this natural gem offers not only a long beach 1 kilometer in length, but all the amenities a tourist might need.

Regarding surfing, it has at least four waves, capable of satisfying a beginner or an expert. The first is known as El Recodo, and it is found at the eastern end of the beach. It is a rocky formation at the mouth of a small river, which produces a short, very fast, steep wave with a tubular section.

The next wave, toward the west, is also a rocky formation, which produces two waves: one breaks gently to the right, making it a friendly and easy wave to ride; and a wave to the left, which is a bit faster and more demanding. In this section it is important to go out at high tide, because the rocks are large and protrude from the water at low tide.

The next wave further west is a left-breaking wave, something rare in the “paradise of right waves,” formed by the combination of a boulder field and the wreck of the merchant ship San Blas, which ran aground there in 1901; this wave can become truly powerful and high-quality, with walls up to 6 feet (2 meters), long lines and tubular sections, suitable for an expert level.

From here up to the junction with El Majahual beach to the west, there is a wide beach break formed by sandbanks that produce different types of waves; some fast and tubular, very good for body surfing, and others foamy but strong, ideal for beginners.

In San Blas there are at least two surf schools, where you can also rent boards for a modest price.

The beach offers many attractions, such as its natural, clean and safe atmosphere. On the shore there are private ranches, many of them for rent; beach clubs, thatched shelters and various types of lodging. There are also public areas for parking and accessing the beach, so anyone can enjoy this paradise.

The long strip of volcanic black sand invites you to set up an umbrella and spend a spectacular day. Walking, running, playing soccer or volleyball, flying a kite or sunbathing and taking a swim are ideal activities for this beach.

You can also observe different bird species, and sightings of sea turtles that come to the coast to nest are common.

If you are going to San Blas from San Salvador, head to the road to the Port of La Libertad, take the bypass Camino a Surf City and then take the Litoral road westward; on your right, at kilometer 39 ½, you will see the wide paved street that leads directly to this lovely destination.

Las Flores beach is located in the department of San Miguel. The small and beautiful cove that welcomes the traveler marks the beginning of a series of rocky points, with right-breaking waves perfect for surfing, that stretch one after another for several kilometers, from the east of the Salvadoran coast toward the west.
It is known as “El Oriente Salvaje” because of its nature, but also because it is remote. Today, modern roads and paths lead to Las Flores, whose natural charm and wave quality remain intact.
During the months of December and January, this beach offers gentle waves, suitable for beginners and intermediate surfers; but when the swells from the southern Pacific Ocean arrive, especially between March and October, you must be prepared, as this point produces waves up to 12 feet high (4 meters), with long, steep faces that move quickly over a semi-rocky bottom until they merge with the volcanic gray sand of its shoreline.
Las Flores is also a picturesque and dramatic setting. While you are there, the immense cliffs that enclose this beautiful beach will undoubtedly catch your eye, with charming hotels built on their summits.
You will also see how the small boats of local fishermen gather side by side on the beach, waiting to head out to sea; or returning to the coast, loaded with the day’s catch. These same vessels are offered to surfers and tourists to transport them to the other waves and deserted beaches visible on the horizon.
The lodging options are broad and varied, both at Las Flores beach and in the nearby community of El Cuco. You can even choose to camp and enjoy a more adventurous experience.
In the area you can taste the local cuisine, from a typical Salvadoran breakfast with eggs, beans and fried plantains; to elaborate seafood dishes.
Getting to Las Flores is easy: From San Salvador take the Pan-American Highway toward San Vicente, then take El Playón street to join the El Litoral road toward San Miguel; upon reaching the El Delirio turnoff, follow the road to El Cuco and Las Flores.

El Tunco beach (a very Salvadoran word for referring to pigs) is the most iconic surf destination in El Salvador.
Its name comes from an immense rock, half-submerged in its beach, which in some remote era suggested the shape of this friendly animal.
Visited weekly by hundreds of local and foreign tourists, the place that in the seventies and eighties was a small hamlet beside a tranquil estuary has become a mandatory pilgrimage point for international surfers and those who seek to immerse themselves in the bohemian, carefree surf culture.
Located just 7 kilometers west of the port of La Libertad, El Tunco is a microcosm where a cosmopolitan atmosphere is felt, fun abounds, and the “chiva” vibe, local slang for something awesome, prevails.
The warmth, familiarity, and service spirit of its people are the cherry on top.
This surf community offers everything imaginable for a spectacular trip.
Modest hostels for backpackers, as well as options for those who want something much more exclusive and private.
Food of every aroma and flavor, from typical pupusas and Salvadoran pastelitos cooked and sold right on the street, to home-cooked meals, elaborate seafood dishes, Asian, Mexican, Mediterranean cuisine, pizzas, burgers, and more.
Local beers and brews from far-flung corners of the world are always served ice-cold. Bars and nightclubs serve all kinds of cocktails.
If you want to taste the best coffee in El Salvador, you’ll find it here.
There are convenience stores and small pharmacies.
Travel agencies arrange your return transportation home or your next destination.
You can also board microbuses that travel throughout Central America.
Parking is available for you to leave your car.
But above all, the surf vibe is in this place’s DNA.
Local surfers, with long hair, tanned skin, and perpetual smiles, mingle with every imaginable race that arrives at this mecca smelling of sea and wax.
Small shops provide surf equipment, clothing, and accessories.
There are craft stalls so you can take home a souvenir of El Salvador, and other forms of street art.
Surf-board rental shops abound, while instructors offer introductions to the warm waves.
In El Tunco you can rent a bicycle, a scooter, or a car, and if you prefer, there are drivers who will take you wherever you want and then safely return you to your lodging.
Because it serves as a kind of connection hub in the area, El Tunco can be your organization and departure point for countless adventure, city, culinary, and other tours.
Above all, this is a small world that screams surf, in its architecture, designs, colors, murals, clothing, and where you breathe that vibe of a world that moves slowly and invites you to be who you are.
Speaking of surf, El Tunco has its own.
The highest-quality wave is La Bocana. A natural left, rare on a coast of right-hand waves, formed by the rocky bottom at the mouth of the Río Grande. It is a powerful break that holds waves up to 10 feet high (3.5 meters), with thick, heavy lips, long lines, and sometimes tubular sections. Suitable only for advanced and expert surfers, it breaks consistently almost year-round.
On each side of the famous rock, where you can’t help but take a photo, there are two sections that throw much smaller, friendlier waves, perfect for beginners; but on epic days they can also show that surfing in El Salvador is world-class.
If you want to visit El Tunco from San Salvador, take the road to the port of La Libertad, then the bypass Camino a Surf City, and continue west on the Litoral highway to kilometer 43, where you’ll see the entrance marked with this famous spot.

Your compact territory, great biodiversity, and the close proximity of natural destinations allow you to experience incredible bird-watching in a short time. In addition, its location on the migratory route of the American continent makes it a privileged point for discovering resident and migratory species year-round.

With more than 500 recorded species, the country offers ideal settings for nature lovers. Cloud forests, mangroves, volcanoes, lakes, and coasts host hummingbirds, toucans, trogons, herons, hawks, pelicans, ibises, and many migratory birds that arrive from North America. Favorable climate and the presence of specialized local guides make each tour even more enriching.

Among the most notable destinations is the Apaneca–Ilamatepec mountain range, famous for its abundance of hummingbirds and high-altitude forest birds. Its mountains, coffee farms, and natural trails provide a perfect environment for exploring while observing birds in freedom.

The Montecristo National Park also stands out, a primary forest of great ecological value where uncommon species live. Likewise, the Bay of Jiquilisco, recognized as a Ramsar site and biosphere reserve, is ideal for observing aquatic and migratory birds among vibrant mangroves.

The Salvadoran coast also holds natural gems such as Barra de Santiago, perfect for spotting marine and migratory birds. Very close, Lake Coatepeque offers spectacular landscapes where aquatic birds and the volcanic setting create ideal scenes for nature photography.

More than a tourist activity, bird-watching in El Salvador drives biodiversity conservation and the development of local communities. Each outing is an invitation to explore, learn, and marvel at the fascinating world of birds.

El Sunzal is, almost certainly, the beach where surfing was first practiced in El Salvador.
Since the first North American surfers arrived in the late 1960s, searching for the perfect wave, this very long right-hand point break has been the favorite of locals and foreigners alike, due to its huge area, which can accommodate dozens of surfers at the same time, and especially its consistency, as it never stops breaking any day of the year.

One of its characteristics is the long paddle required to reach the main breaking spot. It is more than 300 meters of effort, along a friendly channel that, however, can generate a strong side current on big-wave days.

El Sunzal has two perfectly defined sections: the “outside,” located at the farthest part of the coast, where a powerful wave is born that will run continuously for almost 200 meters, offering an endless line and a wide wall for all kinds of maneuvers, delighting both longboarders, shortboarders, and boogie boarders alike. Then there is the “inside,” or middle part, which usually throws its own series of waves, or continues the outer wave; when that happens, the ride from the bottom can be up to 300 meters, with about 40 seconds of pure joy and adrenaline.

El Sunzal is the break that holds the biggest waves of the entire Salvadoran coast, without closing. There have been occasions of extraordinary swells, where perfectly aligned waves up to 25 feet high (8.5 meters) have been seen and ridden. Waves of 8 to 15 feet high (2.5 to 5 meters) are also common, especially between March and October, caused by storms in the southern Pacific Ocean. Among these swells, El Sunzal usually offers a friendly side, making it a favorite wave for beginners.

The rocky bottom provides enough depth to feel safe, although the wave’s “revolcones” are famous; they can be massive and keep you underwater, like a washing machine, for 5 or more painful and endless seconds.

El Sunzal works on all tides, but it is best at mid-tide.

Because of its similarity to some California waves, such as Rincón, El Sunzal and Punta Roca were, in 1977, part of the locations for the iconic surf movie *Big Wednesday* (El verano de mi juventud), which featured stars like Jean Michael Vincent, Gary Busey, and William Katt; and whose surf doubles were the famous surfers Gerry Lopez, Peter Townend, and Ian Cairns, who have never stopped praising the quality of these waves.

During a surf session at El Sunzal, sightings of birds, sea turtles, stingrays, and fish are common. Receiving the sun or witnessing a sunset from the water is often a spiritual experience, especially if there is a moon or a rainbow on the horizon.

Because of its proximity to El Tunco beach, and its own popularity, there are dozens of hotels, hostels, and rental houses in the area, as well as restaurants, bars, convenience stores, and other tourism services.

Local photographers and places that rent surfboards are plentiful, as are instructors who will gladly introduce you to the sport, in one of the undoubtedly most famous, cosmopolitan, and friendly spots in El Salvador.

The easiest way to access El Sunzal is to walk from El Tunco. At certain times of the year the beach can be full of rocks, so an alternative is to go down from one of the restaurants or hotels facing the point, where for a couple of dollars or a day pass you can also have a table, food, drinks, and fresh-water showers.

To get from San Salvador to El Sunzal, simply travel the road to Puerto de La Libertad, cut across the bypass Camino a Surf City, and when you connect with the Litoral road, continue westward to kilometer 43 ½.

Test your endurance by reaching the summit of Ilamatepec volcano, also called Santa Ana volcano. If you manage to get to the highest point you’ll have the most spectacular views of the area; in the distance you’ll see the turquoise waters of the majestic Coatepeque lake.

Located in the department of Santa Ana, the colossus rises 2,381 meters above sea level, making it the highest volcano in El Salvador, with its last eruptions recorded in 2005.

It is part of the Los Volcanes Complex in the Apaneca mountain range, within a tropical montane cloud forest, in a coffee-growing region about 65 kilometers west of the capital.

The main activities of the region are agriculture and tourism, so you won’t regret the landscapes you’ll see as you travel the road, as well as the fruit-selling stalls that characterize the area.

Once you start climbing the volcano, the experience with the flora and fauna will be incredible, also offering you a fresh and delightful climate.

The ascent is of medium difficulty (5/10), with variable weather. Hikers recommend: comfortable clothing, water, sunglasses, sunscreen, a cap or hat, and appropriate footwear for mountaineering or hiking.

Admission to the Complex is $1.50 for Salvadorans; foreigners pay $3.

Children under 6 and adults over 60 enter free.

Hours of operation are from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

¡Juayúa, a destination of landscapes and adventure!
In the midst of mountains and spectacular scenery lies Juayúa, another municipality of the Ruta de Las Flores, waiting for you with cool weather, full of landscapes and natural destinations in Sonsonate, in the western part of El Salvador.
The Seven Waterfalls, where you can climb or rappel on more than one; the Las Ranas lagoon, which is located in the Protected Natural Area of the same name; and Portezuelo Park, an ecological park in the middle of a misty forest are destinations you can enjoy in Juayúa.
You can also take tours of the city on horseback, in carriages, or by train.
In the historic center you will find craft shops, cafés, nurseries, restaurants, art galleries, and on weekends you can taste different dishes at its famous food festival.
You cannot miss visiting the church dedicated to the miraculous Black Christ, its beautiful and historic architecture, a draw for both locals and foreigners.

The Joya de Cerén Archaeological Park is an icon of pre-Hispanic culture that shows you what daily life was like for the Maya. It was declared a World Heritage Site in 1993, and it is called the Pompeii of the Americas, in comparison to the archaeological site in Italy, making it an unmissable destination in El Salvador.
It is unique in El Salvador for having evidence of everyday life of Mesoamerican inhabitants from more than 1,500 years ago, and it also boasts an excellent state of preservation of ancient plants and wildlife.
According to the Ministry of Culture, the village that lived there was buried by the eruption of the Loma Caldera volcano, around 650 C.E. Because of this natural event, the structures and archaeological remains are intact and in good condition. Touring this place full of history is an experience you will not regret.
A fun fact is that the new town of Joya de Cerén, located less than 1 kilometer from the discovered structures, is mostly made up of farmers who use techniques similar to those of the ancient inhabitants, and they offer you their products and clay crafts.
Open Monday through Sunday, from 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

Just 40 minutes from the capital, shopping or tasting dishes made with fresh seafood guarantees one of the best culinary experiences at Mercado del Mar.
The market has 20 restaurants waiting for you with special seafood dishes and à la carte meals. And with the new Camino a Surf City, traffic is a thing of the past, making a family trip even easier.
At this beachfront destination you’ll also find refreshing snacks and coconuts, crafts, and typical “antojitos”; you can also see the full variety of fresh seafood up close and buy whatever you like.
Discover this spot with your family and friends, enjoying a good rest, tasty food, music, and the sea breeze that adorns this place.

A few minutes from the capital, you can find the largest lake in El Salvador. It is of volcanic origin and is ideal for scuba diving, paddle-surfing, kayaking, jet skiing, swimming, boat rides, fishing, or simply taking a dip.
In its surroundings you can go hiking or horseback riding. Camp or spend an unforgettable night in a rental house, hostel, or hotel.
A plus of the lake is that, around its shores, there are themed restaurants with spectacular views. The Panoramic Route is recommended, where the dining options are varied and perfect for having good times and capturing unforgettable images.
